turns.text: Okay, Elias, Mom, welcome back. Let's look at the week. I've got the log up here. Elias, have you seen what your mom's been writing?
Some of it. Her spelling is really bad.
I type with one thumb in the pickup line. Give me a break.

I can read it fine, don't worry. So a lot of entries about group chats, a few about lunch, and the basketball tryout. Let's start with the chats, since there are the most of those. Elias, what's going on with the group chats?
Nothing. I muted the class one.
What made you mute it?
It's just everybody talking. Like forty messages about nothing. And if I say something it just sits there.
Sits there?
Like nobody answers. And then it's just your message hanging there with everybody seeing it and nobody saying anything.
And what does it mean, when nobody answers?
That they think I'm annoying. Or like, why is he even in here.
Okay. That's a pretty painful thing to imagine. Has that happened? You sent something and nobody answered?
Once. In sixth grade. But that was a different chat.
So once, a while ago. And now when you do send something, like the science project chat, Mom wrote that you showed her the message a few times first.
Four times. Five maybe. And then the birthday one, it was literally three words, sure I'm in, and he asked me if it sounded okay.
Because it might sound like I'm too excited. Or not excited enough.
And I tell him it's fine. Every time. Because it is fine.

It is fine. And here's the thing I want both of you to notice. Elias asks, Mom says it's fine, Elias feels better for about a minute. And then the next message, he needs to ask again. The checking works right then, but it doesn't stick. It's a bit like scratching a bug bite.
So I should just not ask?
We'll get there in small pieces. First let me get a number. Zero to ten, how scary is sending a message in a group chat, without showing anyone first?
Without showing? Like a six.
Six. And Mom, you had fives and sixes on there, so that fits. Okay, lunch. Elias, tell me about lunch.
I'm not hungry at lunch. It's early. It's like eleven.
He's not hungry at eleven, but he is starving at three o'clock. And he asked me to stop packing sandwiches. Just crackers and cheese.
What's wrong with sandwiches?
They're messy. Stuff falls out. And people are right there.
People are right there. And you sit at the end of the table, Mom mentioned.
Yeah. It's just better at the end.
What would happen if you sat in the middle with a sandwich?
I don't know. I just don't like it.
That's okay, you don't have to know yet. How about a number? Eating lunch at school, with people around, zero to ten.
Seven.
Seven. Thanks, Elias. And then there was basketball. Do you want to tell it or should Mom?
He went. I want to say that first, he went. He wanted to try out. And they did warm-ups, and then he texted me that he felt sick, and I went and picked him up.
I did feel sick.
I believe you. Anxiety can make your stomach feel really sick. What was going on right before you texted?
They were about to do shooting. Like one at a time, with the coach watching, and everyone in a line behind you.
And what did you think would happen when it was your turn?
That I'd miss. And everyone would see. And laugh.
How high was it, right then, in the gym?
Nine. Like a full nine.
That's what I wrote too.
A nine is a lot. And you walked into that gym and did the whole warm-up. Tryouts are done for this year, right?
Yeah. They posted the list.

Okay. So we're not going to plan anything around basketball right now. We'll keep it on the list for later. Let's pick the thing with the most chances to practice, and that's the group chats, since you're in them every day.
Okay.
Here's my idea. Once a day, you send one message in a group chat. It can be short. Lol counts. A thumbs up doesn't count, it has to be words. And you don't show it to Mom first.
Once a day? In the class one?
Any group chat. Doesn't have to be the class one. You pick. And then, the part that matters most, you don't check it again for ten minutes. You just put the phone down.
What if nobody answers?

Then you write that down. That's the experiment. We find out what actually happens, instead of guessing. Mom, here's your part. When he asks you if a message sounds okay, you say, I think you can decide. Kindly. And that's it. You don't read it.
Even if he really wants me to?
Even then. That'll be the hard part for you. You can tell him you know it's hard.
Okay. I think you can decide. I can say that.
What if I send something and it's actually bad? Like it actually sounds dumb?
Good question. What do you think would happen?
Somebody would screenshot it. Or nobody would say anything, which is worse.
Okay. So the worst one is nobody says anything. Let me ask you this. When somebody else in that chat sends a message and nobody answers, what do you think about them?
I don't think anything. I probably don't even see it. There's like a hundred messages.
Huh. So when it's someone else, the message just goes by and you don't notice. But when it's yours, it hangs there and everyone sees it.
Yeah. I know that doesn't make sense.

It makes a lot of sense, actually. That's how worry works. It puts a spotlight on you that nobody else is holding. The messages this week are a way to check whether the spotlight is real. You keep track, and next week we look at it together. How many got answers, how many didn't, and what happened after.
Should he write that down, or should I?
Elias, would you be willing to keep a little note on your phone? Just the date, and whether anyone answered. Mom, you keep doing the log the way you have been, with the number.
On my phone? Fine. As long as she doesn't read it.
She won't read it. It's yours. You can show me next week, or just tell me what's in it.
I won't read it. I promise. I'm going to have enough trouble with I think you can decide.

One more thing on lunch, Mom. I know it's hard to see the lunch box come home full. For this week, I'd ask you not to change anything about lunch. Don't add sandwiches back, don't take crackers away. Just write down what comes home. We'll come back to lunch soon. I'd rather do one thing well than three things halfway.
Okay. Crackers and cheese, no changes, write it down.
And keep logging. For the chats, the number before he sends it. Lunch, just keep noting what comes home, no changes there yet. Elias, are you in?
Sure, I'm in.
Was that too excited?
Mom.
